highlights.text: yielding a single core notion: al-shahwa, meaning appetite, craving, or desire.
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's single core notion for the root

highlights.text: The shared idea has two strands: (a) one thing interpenetrating another, part entering part; and (b) height and elevation.
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris: two strands, one shared idea

highlights.text: شَجَر — trees / woody plants. Singular شَجَرَة (a tree), which always involves height and interlacing branches.
شَجَرَ بَيْنَ الْقَوْمِ — a matter arises in dispute among people
its one meaning is interpenetration: one thing entering into another
al-shakk, the opposite of certainty (yaqīn), belongs here
the doubter is as if two matters had been skewered together for him
highlights.note: why doubt belongs to this root

highlights.text: In a verse of Dhū al-Rumma describing a scarred wild ass leaping "as though he had a manifest shakk or were afflicted in the side"
highlights.note: Dhū al-Rumma, Umayyad; the entry has no earlier witness

highlights.text: matching, resembling, binding/hobbling
highlights.note: the entry's core idea for the root

highlights.text: Cited for Q38:58, "others of its kind, in pairs" — meaning resembling something else in form and in the act performed.
Shākila (Q17:84, "each works according to his shākila"): means one's innate disposition (sajiyya)
"people are kinds, and they pair up with their own kind" (al-nāsu ashkālun wa-allāf)
He likens this to a saying attributed to the Prophet: "Everyone is made easy toward that for which he was created."
highlights.note: a hadith, used to explain shākila in Q 17:84

highlights.text: four separate roots that, in his view, share no common underlying sense.
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris: the four roots share no common sense

highlights.text: Shukr — praise or thanks given to a person for a kindness done to you.
a line of al-Aʿshā describing a summer raid so harsh it exhausts even a hardy, easily-kept mare
al-shikis/al-shakas — bad-tempered, difficult in dealing (mubāyaʿah) and otherwise
al-Zumar 39:29: "shurakāʾu mutashākisūn" — quarrelling partners
شِكاية is the making-visible of inward distress (بَثّ). Its origin is "opening the شَكْوة" — a small skin water-bag — and showing what is inside
highlights.note: al-Rāghib on the word's origin, via al-Zabīdī

highlights.text: شَكَا (imperfect يَشْكو) — "he laid his case before God," i.e. he informed Him of the weakness of his condition
شَكَى فلاناً — to report the wrong someone has done to you.
Qurʾānic citations given: "I only complain of my anguish and grief to God" and "and she complains to God."
A recess or window in a wall that does not pass through
al-Ṭirimmāḥ: "My mark is complained of and my tongue is fierce."
highlights.note: al-Ṭirimmāḥ, Umayyad; the entry's only named poet

highlights.text: "We complained to the Messenger of God of the burning ground against our foreheads, and he did not relieve us," i.e. did not remove the grievance
highlights.note: a hadith, cited for the privative sense of أَشْكى

highlights.text: the majority (Ibn Jubayr, Saʿīd b. ʿIyāḍ) take it as the blind wall-recess, which concentrates light so a lamp shines brighter there
highlights.note: exegetes Ibn Jubayr and Saʿīd b. ʿIyāḍ on Q 24:35

highlights.text: Kaʿb's reading takes the niche as Muḥammad's breast, the lamp his tongue, the glass his mouth
highlights.note: Kaʿb's exegesis of Q 24:35, via al-Suhaylī

highlights.text: encircling something and taking hold of it from every side
the side opposite the right
اليد الشِّمال — the left hand.
شَمَلَهُمُ الأمر — a matter "encompassed" them
Plural of شِمال is أشْمُل (shāhid: Abū al-Najm, "it comes to it from rights and lefts")
highlights.note: Abū al-Najm, Umayyad; the entry has no earlier witness

highlights.text: A verse of Dhū al-Rumma on "the shamāʾil of Jillān" is read two ways
changeableness and restlessness — something that shifts and will not stay put
al-shams (the sun): named from this idea because it never stays fixed but is always in motion
He supports this with the Qur'anic reading "and the sun runs — no fixed resting-place of its own."
highlights.note: the entry's own reading of the Qur'anic verse

highlights.text: شَمِتَ بِهِ (shamita bihi) = "he gloated over him," rejoicing at a calamity that has struck someone hostile to him.
He cites Qur'an 7:150, {فَلَا تُشْمِتْ بِيَ الْأَعْدَاءَ}, "so let not the enemies gloat over me," as an instance of this root.
A poetic line is quoted: a man startled by hunting hounds spends the night "at the mercy of the gloaters, from fear and from cold."
highlights.note: unattributed verse; the entry names no poet here

highlights.text: Ibn Fāris quotes a ḥadīth: two men sneezed before the Prophet; he gave the blessing (tashmīt) to one but not the other, explaining that the first had said "al-ḥamdu lillāh" (praised God) and the second had not.
highlights.note: a hadith, the source of the tashmīt al-ʿāṭis sense

highlights.text: a single core sense: self-magnification paired with physical height
jabalun shāmikh, "a lofty/towering mountain," meaning ʿālin, "high."
The verb ishmaʾazza — used, the text says, "when it contracts" (idhā taqabbaḍa), i.e., to describe something drawing itself together or shrinking/recoiling.
The root points to *bighḍa* (hatred) and to turning away from a thing.
شَنَآن (*shanaʾān*), sometimes lightened (hamza dropped) to شَنَان (*shanān*).
"Life is only what you enjoy and desire, even if the man of hatred blames you for it and calls you a fool."
highlights.note: unattributed verse, using the lightened شَنَان

highlights.text: one sound root meaning a splitting open in a thing, with further words derived from it by metaphor.
shaqaqtu al-shayʾ, ashuqquhu, shaqqan: "I split the thing", when you cleave it.
al-shiqāq is disagreement: the community cracks and divides.
shiqq and mashaqqa are severe difficulty, as if its severity splits a person.
al-shuqqa is a long journey to a distant land, "an arduous shuqqa"
Labīd uses the word of a wild cow that lost her calf and kept roaming and lowing "across the breadth of the shaqāʾiq"
Al-Aʿshā: "I cut off the shiqshiqa of the roarer."
the side of a mountain, as in the ḥadīth "he found me among owners of a few sheep at a shiqq"
highlights.note: a hadith, cited for shiqq = mountainside

highlights.text: sh-q-w point to hardship and suffering — the opposite of ease
رَجُلٌ شَقِيٌّ (shaqiyy) is a wretched, hard-pressed man
So الشِّقْوَة (shiqwah) means the opposite of felicity.
a piece torn/separated off from a whole
a group that is broken off or detached — a small, cut-off band.
ثوبٌ شَرَاذِمُ (a garment [that is] shirdhim/sharādhim)
a core idea he states plainly: something that is opened up, with an extension or stretch to it
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris states the core image plainly

highlights.text: الشَّرِيعَة (sharīʿa) is the place of access to water where the drinker comes down to drink.
From that watering-place sense, Ibn Fāris says, شِرْعَة (shirʿa) and شَرِيعَة were derived for what pertains to الدِّين (dīn).
highlights.note: شِرْعَة 1x, شَرِيعَة 1x: derived from the water sense

highlights.text: حِيتَانٌ شُرَّعٌ — fish lowering their heads to drink.
رُمْحٌ شِرَاعِيٌّ, "a long spear," in a line attributed to al-Hudhalī
Q 7:163 (fish coming "shurraʿan" on the Sabbath day) is glossed by some exegetes as "raising their heads."
highlights.note: a gloss by unnamed exegetes on Q 7:163

highlights.text: a minor root (uṣayl) pointing to "opening" (fatḥ) and "making evident" (bayān).
highlights.note: Ibn Fāris's minor root: opening, making evident

highlights.text: sharaḥtu al-kalāma wa-ghayrahu sharḥan, "I explained speech, or something else"
highlights.note: شَرَحَ 5x: the root's ordinary sense of laying open

highlights.text: a sign or mark (ʿalāma/ʿalam), and anything that approximates a sign.
al-sharaṭ = "sign, mark." Ashrāṭ al-sāʿa, "the signs of the Hour," takes its name from this
(Also: ashrāṭ al-sāʿa is said to mean its earliest portents.)
highlights.note: a second gloss of the Qur'anic ashrāṭ

highlights.text: A verse of Ḥassān [ibn Thābit] uses ashrāṭ for companions "roused after the slumber-time of al-ashrāṭ"
highlights.note: Ḥassān ibn Thābit, lived into Islam

highlights.text: The base sense is consuming any liquid, water or otherwise.
the Garden's people are given "a pure drink" (Q76:21), the Fire's people "a drink of scalding water" (Q10:4)
A distinct vocalization meaning one's turn or portion of water
the noun of the place of drinking (a drinking-place)
ashrabtanī mā lam ashrab, "you made me drink what I did not drink" — i.e., you alleged against me what I never did.
(b) The love of the calf was "made to be drunk into" their hearts.
scaring or driving something away to a distance
sharradtu al-ibila tashridan — "I scattered/drove off the camels."
{fa-sharrid bihim man khalfahum}, "so by them, scatter/disperse those behind them."
highlights.note: the Qur'anic form in its ordinary sense

highlights.text: Ibn Faris glosses this as nakkil bihim wa-sammi' — "make an exemplary, deterrent punishment of them, and publicize it"
highlights.note: the author's own exegesis of Q 8:57

highlights.text: shirka (partnership): a thing held between two people, with neither possessing it by himself.
ashraktu fulānan = "I made him my partner (sharīk)."
highlights.note: أَشْرَكَ 71x, شَرِيك 40x: the entry's literal sense

highlights.text: "and make him a sharer in my affair" (Ṭā-Hā 32)
a single root meaning illumination and opening
شَرَقَتِ الشَّمْسُ (sharaqat al-shams) = the sun rose; أَشْرَقَتْ (ashraqat) = it gave light
الْمَشْرِقَانِ (the two easts) = the sun's rising-points in summer and winter
spreading out and flying about
al-sharr is the opposite of khayr (good); a wicked man is shirrīr.
sharāra (plural sharār) and sharar (singular sharara) are what flies up from fire, as in Q 77:32
Ṭarafa: "my drinking of wine went on until my friend imputed evil to me"
Imruʾ al-Qays, passing guards and men eager against him, "if only they could bring my death out into the open"
analyzes the root sh-r-ā (shīn + rāʾ + a weak final letter) as three distinct roots.
شَرَى / اشْتَرَى (sharā / ishtarā): to take a thing from its owner for a price, i.e. to buy.
Qur'an 12:20, {وَشَرَوْهُ بِثَمَنٍ بَخْسٍ}, "they sold him for a paltry price."
"كل مُجْرٍ في الخلاء يشرى" — "anyone racing in open, empty ground grows spirited/reckless."
Illustrated by a saying of the judge Shurayḥ about a man who broke another's bow — he ruled "شَرْوَاهَا," its equivalent (in compensation).
highlights.note: a judge's ruling, giving sharwā a legal use
